baseline: Host LTP 20260529 binary /nix/store/hik6kb512ia3p14lc2vwzb292d4k306a-ltp-20260529/testcases/bin/timerfd_gettime01 passes 3/3 (one variant only: x86_64 has no __NR_timerfd_gettime64, so the time64 variant is compiled out). Per assertion, the correct kernel returns: case 1 (fd = -1, curr_value = NULL) -> EBADF; case 2 (valid timerfd fd, curr_value = tst_get_bad_addr() PROT_NONE page) -> EFAULT; case 3 (regular-file fd from SAFE_OPEN, curr_value = NULL) -> EINVAL. Note cases 1 and 3 both pass NULL, since tst_its_get(NULL) returns NULL (include/tst_timer.h:188-191); only the EFAULT case substitutes bad_addr (timerfd_gettime01.c:75-78). A direct 10-case host probe (/tmp/tfg_probe.c) pins the full ordering rather than just these three: fd errors always win over pointer errors, and the fd-type error wins over the pointer error. -1+NULL -> EBADF, -1+badptr -> EBADF, -1+goodptr -> EBADF, unallocated fd 1500+NULL -> EBADF, regular fd+NULL -> EINVAL, regular fd+badptr -> EINVAL, regular fd+goodptr -> EINVAL, valid timerfd+badptr -> EFAULT, valid timerfd+NULL -> EFAULT, valid timerfd+goodptr -> 0. So NULL is never special-cased: it is simply an unwritable address, and it yields EFAULT only once the fd has been proven to be a timerfd.
failing_assertion: timerfd_gettime01.c:91: TFAIL: timerfd_gettime() failed unexpectedly; expected: 9 - Bad file descriptor: EINVAL (22) -- case 1 (fd = -1, curr_value = NULL). Asterinas returns EINVAL (22) where Linux returns EBADF (9). Asterinas run at base e8f2b9ca6: 2 passed / 1 failed / 0 broken / 0 skipped, vs host 3/0/0/0. The other two cases pass, but case 3 passes coincidentally: it also lands on the same early NULL check and gets EINVAL by accident rather than from the timerfd type check that Linux uses.
root_cause: sys_timerfd_gettime in kernel/src/syscall/timerfd_gettime.rs opens with a hand-rolled NULL-pointer guard at lines 17-19 -- `if itimerspec_addr == 0 { return_errno_with_message!(Errno::EINVAL, "invalid pointer to return value") }` -- and that guard runs before the fd is ever looked at. The fd resolution that would produce EBADF sits after it at lines 21-23 (`raw_fd.try_into()?` then `file_table_locked.get_file(...)`). So for case 1 the syscall returns from line 18 without touching raw_fd at all, and the -1 never reaches the conversion that would reject it. Every downstream piece is already correct and unreachable for this input: TryFrom<RawFileDesc> for FileDesc rejects negative fds with EBADF (kernel/src/fs/file/file_table.rs:92-97), FileTable::get_file supplies EBADF for unallocated fds (file_table.rs:237-242), the downcast_ref::<TimerfdFile>() at lines 24-26 already yields EINVAL for a non-timerfd, and write_val at line 33 already yields EFAULT for address 0 -- CurrentUserSpace::write calls check_vaddr_lowerbound (kernel/src/context.rs:244-254, 273-278), which returns ostd::Error::PageFault for any va < VMAR_LOWEST_ADDR, and error.rs:203 maps PageFault to Errno::EFAULT. The guard is therefore not merely mis-ordered, it is redundant: it hard-codes the wrong errno for a condition the generic user-copy path already reports correctly as EFAULT. It has been there since the syscall was introduced in 1775bb086 ("Support for timerfd-related syscalls"); nothing regressed it.
invariant: A syscall that takes both a file descriptor and a user-space pointer must fully validate the descriptor -- existence, then type -- before it dereferences or validates the pointer, so that fd errors (EBADF, then EINVAL for the wrong file type) always take precedence over pointer errors (EFAULT). Corollary: a null pointer is not a distinct error condition to be special-cased; it is an unmapped address, and the generic user-copy path must be the single place that reports it, as EFAULT.
owning_layer: The syscall entry layer -- argument-validation ordering inside the sys_* handler in kernel/src/syscall/timerfd_gettime.rs. This is where the ordering contract belongs in Asterinas, because Asterinas has no per-syscall argument-marshalling layer between the dispatch table (kernel/src/syscall/arch/x86.rs:397) and the handler body; the handler *is* the entry layer. The two collaborators it must sequence correctly are already the right abstractions and need no change: the fd layer (TryFrom<RawFileDesc>/FileTable::get_file for EBADF, downcast_ref::<TimerfdFile>() for EINVAL) and the user-memory layer (CurrentUserSpace::write_val/check_vaddr_lowerbound for EFAULT). The fix is to delete the hand-rolled guard so both layers are reached in the correct order, not to add a check anywhere else. Fixing this by, say, teaching write_val to return EINVAL for address 0 would be a patch at the wrong layer: it would paper over this test while corrupting EFAULT reporting for every other syscall.
linux_reference: fs/timerfd.c. Linux enforces this ordering structurally, by splitting the work across two functions. do_timerfd_gettime(int ufd, struct itimerspec64 *t) does all fd validation against a kernel-side itimerspec64: `CLASS(fd, f)(ufd); if (fd_empty(f)) return -EBADF; if (fd_file(f)->f_op != &timerfd_fops) return -EINVAL;` -- and only then reads the timer. The user pointer is not visible to it. SYSCALL_DEFINE2(timerfd_gettime, int, ufd, struct __kernel_itimerspec __user *, otmr) is the wrapper: it calls do_timerfd_gettime(ufd, &kt) first and only afterwards does put_itimerspec64(&kt, otmr), which is the sole source of EFAULT. There is no NULL check on otmr anywhere -- copy_to_user handles address 0 like any other bad address. Pre-6.12 trees used a timerfd_fget(fd, &f) helper wrapping the same two checks in the same order; Al Viro folded it into the callers in "timerfd: switch to CLASS(fd, ...)" (landed 6.12) with error semantics unchanged. do_timerfd_settime uses the identical check pattern, which is why timerfd_settime(-1, ..., NULL, NULL) returns EFAULT on the host while timerfd_settime(-1, ..., &good, NULL) returns EBADF -- settime reads its input pointer, so the precedence there is fd-then-pointer too, just with a read instead of a write.
other_callers: Nobody else calls sys_timerfd_gettime -- it is a syscall entry point, reached only from the x86 dispatch table at kernel/src/syscall/arch/x86.rs:397 (SYS_TIMERFD_GETTIME = 287), and there is no timerfd_gettime64 entry in the table at all. So the fix is legitimately confined to this one 36-line file. But the *antipattern* is not confined to it, and two siblings carry the same defect measured against the host: sys_timer_gettime (kernel/src/syscall/timer_settime.rs:69-71) NULL-checks with EINVAL before resolving timer_id, where the host returns EFAULT for a valid timer id plus NULL (it returns EINVAL only for a bad id, so Asterinas is right by accident in one case and wrong in the other); and sys_getitimer (kernel/src/syscall/setitimer.rs:85-87) NULL-checks with EINVAL where the host returns EFAULT unconditionally for getitimer(ITIMER_REAL, NULL). Neither is exercised by timerfd_gettime01, so neither should be swept into this fix, but both are the same rule violated in the same way and are candidates for their own rounds. By contrast sys_timerfd_settime (kernel/src/syscall/timerfd_settime.rs) is already correct: it resolves the fd at lines 27-32 before reading the user pointer at line 35, and guards the optional old_itimerspec_addr with `> 0` only to make it genuinely optional, which matches Linux treating a NULL otmr in settime as "do not report the old value".
suggested_direction: Delete the three-line guard at kernel/src/syscall/timerfd_gettime.rs:17-19 outright. Do not relocate it: after deletion the existing sequence is already exactly Linux's order -- raw_fd.try_into()? gives EBADF for -1, get_file gives EBADF for an unallocated fd, downcast_ref::<TimerfdFile>() gives EINVAL for a non-timerfd, and write_val(0, ..) gives EFAULT via check_vaddr_lowerbound. That single deletion turns case 1 from EINVAL to EBADF, keeps case 2 at EFAULT, and re-derives case 3's EINVAL from the type check that Linux uses instead of from a coincidence, so all three assertions pass for the right reason. It also brings the seven ordering combinations the host probe covered beyond the test's three into agreement, including valid-timerfd+NULL -> EFAULT, which the current code gets wrong as EINVAL but which no assertion in this test exercises. Then uncomment line 1715 of test/initramfs/src/conformance/ltp/testcases/all.txt ('# timerfd_gettime01'). Verify with the default configuration -- no CONFORMANCE_TEST_WORKDIR override, run_vars empty -- since the pool entry comes from all.txt.
